content_units: You need to free up   $350/month   without touching   retirement savings   or reducing   debt payments  .
That means cutting   $350 helps, but it will not fully balance the budget  . A fully balanced version needs about   $697   in total reductions.
Here’s the cleanest cut plan for the first   $350  :
Category   Current   Suggested   Cut   Why this is reasonable
Dining out   $340   $220     $120     Biggest flexible area without affecting essentials
Subscriptions   $92   $25     $67     Keeps one streaming service and cuts extras
Entertainment   $210   $140     $70     Still leaves room for fun spending
Clothing   $160   $100     $60     Enough for basics; pause nonessential buys
Option 1:   Balanced trim plan     Hits the $350 target with the least lifestyle disruption     Best fit
Option 2:   More aggressive discretionary reset     Closes more of the full deficit faster     Better if cash flow feels tight
This would cut   $457 total  , leaving a gap of about   $240  .
Option 3:   Full-balance version     Brings the budget roughly to zero without touching retirement or debt     Most practical long-term
This gets you to about   $697+   in cuts, which is what your budget actually needs.
A few categories stand out as the best places to cut first:
-   Dining out ($340):   high enough to trim meaningfully without hurting groceries
-   Subscriptions ($92):   likely more services than needed if keeping only one streamer
-   Entertainment ($210):   still flexible after a reduction
-   Clothing ($160):   can usually be paused short term
Categories I would   leave alone first  :
-   Groceries ($520)   — matches your priority to keep it realistic
-   Debt payment ($300)   — protected by your priority
-   Retirement contribution ($300)   — protected by your priority
-   Rent / utilities / insurance   — less flexible in the short term
Used your stated priorities as hard constraints:
- groceries not used as the main cut source
- one streaming service preserved inside the subscriptions category
